newsitem.title: KENYA: No end in sight to age-old Tutsi-Hutu hatred.
newsitem.headline: No end in sight to age-old Tutsi-Hutu hatred.

text.p: Hutus and Tutsis are imprisoned in one of Africa's bloodiest, most tenacious ethnic feuds which has torn apart Rwanda, ravaged Burundi and now destabilised their giant neighbour, Zaire.

The fresh conflict was sparked when Zaire, home to more than a million Hutu refugees from outside its borders, ordered its indigenous Tutsis -- a tiny proportion of its 40 million people, who say they are victims of a plan of genocide -- to get out.
Before this, however decades of Hutu-Tutsi conflict were centred on their joint heartlands, Rwanda and Burundi.
Their rivalry goes back centuries but its results have grown more horrific as insensitive European rule, post-colonial upheaval and rising populations upset a fragile balance.
The two groups were distinguished by class, history and physique but nevertheless lived together for centuries in their small corner of central Africa.
In both Rwanda and Burundi, Tutsis were the overlords who dominated their Hutu serfs, 85 percent of the population, but despite the rigid divisions intermarriage was common.
The Hutus, darker-skinned, stocky farmers, lived there first. They were conquered about 400 years ago by tall, cattle-keeping Tutsis from the north who set up the twin feudal kingdoms.

German explorer Count von Goetzen described the Tutsis as impressive "with their gigantic stature, the sublimity of their speech, the tasteful and unobtrusive way of their dress, their noble traits and their quiet, penetrating, often even witty and irritating, eyes".
Colonial rulers reinforced the existing social system after the kingdoms were taken over by the Germans, who came in 1899, and later turned over to Belgium as a protectorate after World War I.
The Tutsis, with lighter skin and aquiline features, were favoured by the Belgians.
But colonial disruption eroded the old order and, as independence and democratic elections approached, Hutus and Tutsis took greater refuge in their separate ethnic identities.
Colonialism ended in 1962. The majority Hutus took control of government in Rwanda but were suppressed in Burundi whose Tutsis controlled the army.
Ethnic pogroms flared up at intervals in the ensuing decades in both countries, the most densely populated in Africa, sending waves of refugees into neighbouring states.
The hatred exploded into genocide in 1994 when Hutu militiamen wiped out an estimated nine-tenths of the 930,000 Tutsis living in Rwanda, as well as moderate Hutus, in a two-month frenzy of killing.
It failed to stop a Tutsi rebel army seizing power, and some two million Hutus fled their homeland and are still refugees.
More than 150,000 people have died in civil war and massacres since 1993 in Burundi, controlled by a minority Tutsi regime and the Tutsi-dominated army which toppled the Hutu president in 1993.
Aid workers now fear for the lives of more than a million Hutu refugees from both countries who have fled since 1994 westwards into Zaire but whose camps are caught up in the fresh war there.
Today, most of an estimated two million or so Tutsis live in areas they control.
In Rwanda, several hundred thousand Tutsi refugees from earlier strife have returned from Uganda and Tanzania to join the 130,000 Tutsis who were the only ones to survive the genocide.

Burundi to its south is Tutsi-controlled and now eastern Zaire, to the west, is largely in the hands of the Banyamulenge, descendants of Tutsis who moved to Zaire over the last 200 years and who today number 200,000 to 400,000.

The Hutus, who number approximately 12 million in all, control only the squalid Mugunga refugee camp in Zaire, the world's biggest where over 400,000 desperate Hutus wait for help, and any other camps still holding out against the rebels.
